headline: Obesity may close
body: Through a pathway nobody in this space discusses.
punch: Insulin appears to regulate aromatase inside the cartilage itself.

headline: The known link
body: Heavier children often mature earlier. That usually gets explained through leptin, or through more fat tissue producing more estrogen systemically.
punch: There may be a more local explanation.

headline: Researchers used
body: Juvenile rats made obese and hyperinsulinemic, then examined for whether insulin regulates aromatase expression locally within growth plate cartilage.
punch: The question is about the tissue, not the bloodstream.

headline: Why aromatase
body: Aromatase converts androgens into estrogen, and estrogen is the dominant driver of growth plate closure. Anything raising local aromatase raises local estrogen.
punch: It's the enzyme sitting at the closure switch.

headline: So the proposed chain
body: Obesity raises insulin. Insulin acts on growth plate cartilage. Local aromatase rises. Local estrogen rises. Skeletal maturation accelerates.
punch: Four steps from diet to bone age.

headline: This reframes
body: Heavier children being taller early and not taller finally is usually described as a curiosity. This offers a mechanism for why the early advantage doesn't hold.
punch: Early tall and finally tall are different outcomes.

headline: The evidence limits
body: Rat model, diet-induced obesity, and the study investigates the link rather than settling it. No human growth plate data and no final height outcomes.
punch: A proposed mechanism with animal support.

headline: Why it still matters
body: Metabolic health is modifiable, common, and affects far more people than any compound discussed in this niche. A plausible mechanism there outranks an exotic one elsewhere.
punch: Boring levers move more people than interesting ones.
